pages.title: Week 5 Day 2: build your funnel in a CRM
pages.subtitle: Brianna Salinas, 500 Global | One recording, 20 October 2026 | 1h 01m (55 min lecture, 6 min questions)

blocks.title: The lecture in one sentence
blocks.body: Treat your CRM as the single source of truth: pick a few goals, define 4-7 stages named after what the buyer did, give each stage written exit criteria, keep health in a separate status field, record the few fields your reports need, and review the numbers on a fixed rhythm, so you can answer any investor question from data instead of from memory.

blocks.title: Six points to remember
blocks.body:
1. Use the same words for everyone: contact, lead, prospect (SQL), opportunity, customer. A customer is someone who has signed and is paying (S1 03:07-04:44; slide 5).
2. Goals decide your stages, required fields and reports. Require only what you need, or nobody fills it in, and data is very hard to add later (S1 10:12-14:47; slide 9).
3. Good stages are simple, distinct, easy to log and consistent. Test: would two reps put the same deal in the same stage without asking? (S1 20:24-21:31; slide 10)
4. Every stage exits on something the buyer did. 'Closed won' means a signed contract, nothing less (S1 27:28-29:07; slide 14).
5. Stage is where the deal is; status is how healthy it is. Never make a 'stalled' stage (S1 30:19-31:44; slide 16).
6. Investors trust real numbers: qualified opportunities, conversion from your own history, and honest closed-lost reasons. Free pilots and LOIs are not ARR (S1 50:41-55:03; slides 38-41).

blocks.title: Where MediMind stands
blocks.body: Irakli asked what to do when the CRM 'exists in my head'. Brianna's answer: put everything in a spreadsheet first, then design the stages, and she offered to map our situation in office hours, mentioning '24 hospitals' and 'one customer' (S1 57:13-58:02). We already drafted a 9-step hospital funnel on 2 October. The lecture says 4-7 stages. Pages 12-15 turn it into a 6-stage pipeline with buyer exit criteria, a status field, and investor-safe numbers.
Fast route: this page, page 6 (exit criteria and stage vs status), page 8 (weighted pipeline), page 11 (homework and questions), page 12 (our stages) and page 15 (actions).

blocks.title: Pipeline vs funnel
blocks.body: The pipeline is you moving a deal through your sales stages; it lives in the CRM and is what this lecture is about. The funnel is the wider customer journey (awareness, discovery, evaluation, intent, purchase, loyalty), used more by marketing. Both show where people drop off (S1 04:44-06:09; slide 6).

rows: Sum of each deal x its stage probability (page 8)
# opportunities x win rate x average value / cycle days

blocks.title: Why velocity matters
blocks.body: Velocity is the revenue your pipeline produces per day. 'You can double your pipeline, but if the deals take twice as long to close, you are not getting revenue any faster' (S1 09:14-09:27). Investors ask about metrics 7 and 8 before most founders track them, so learn the formulas now (S1 08:24-08:42).

rows: Which deals stopped moving, and where people drop off
Where your winning deals come from
Which stage slows deals down: a technical step, finding the decision maker?
Customer success gets the full deal history, so the customer never repeats themselves
Investor questions answered with a few months of data

blocks.title: Goals decide the stages, required fields and reports
blocks.body: 'If you require all of the fields, you will probably stop filling them out yourselves as founders, and your sales team will too.' Require only what your goals need. Plan it now, because 'it's very, very hard to go back and add data'. Example: if you never recorded lead source, you cannot say later which July contacts became your best customers (S1 13:23-14:47). In the chat, Irakli's goal was 'increase sales?'; others wanted to keep track of deals and push them forward on time.

blocks.title: Question 1: can we build our own CRM? (a Joberos founder, S1 14:54-17:49)
blocks.body: Yes. HubSpot and Salesforce became overwhelming because they do everything and almost need a consultant. At an early stage, keep it simple, track what your goals need and keep the data clean, so you can move it to a bigger CRM later. Moving between CRMs is common. What matters most is one source of truth, so you never email someone already in a deal or send them irrelevant marketing. Julia built hers in Claude.

blocks.title: Question 2: one CRM for sales and customer success? (Julia, S1 17:52-20:12)
blocks.body: Yes, keep all customer data in one place. People can work in different tools or views as long as everything flows into the one record. The salesperson learns a lot; capture it so the account team can succeed even if that salesperson leaves. Onboarding is next week's topic.

rows: Anyone understands it on day one
No overlap: a deal fits one stage only, never 'maybe demo, maybe proposal'
Moving a deal takes one click; harder logging means messier data and no reports
Everyone, including every new hire, uses it the same way

blocks.title: Three ways to name stages (slide 11)
blocks.body: Seller activity (call booked, demo given, proposal sent): easy, but 'it measures what you did, not where the buyer is'. Buyer commitment (problem confirmed, champion agreed to evaluate, budget and signer confirmed). Best practice: buyer-based names plus written exit criteria, the things that must be true before the deal moves on (S1 21:31-22:50). Avoid the founder habit of making a new stage for every action, '20 sales stages' (S1 23:16).

rows: Appointment scheduled; Qualified to buy; Presentation scheduled; Decision maker bought-in; Contract sent; Closed won; Closed lost
Prospecting; Qualification; Needs analysis; Value proposition; Identify decision makers; Perception analysis; Proposal/price quote; Negotiation/review; Closed won; Closed lost
Lead; Discovery; Demo/pilot; Proposal; Contract sent

blocks.title: Stages change as you grow
blocks.body: GitLab added stage 0, 'pending acceptance', because leads sat unanswered until a rep accepted them. Your stages are for today; six months from now you may add a step, for example for a new market. Start with the minimum you need to see where deals get stuck (S1 24:25-26:15).

blocks.title: Irakli's chat question: are contacts in the CRM before I contact them?
blocks.body: Yes, they can be. Contacts can sit in the CRM without being in the pipeline. A conference list of 50 people is contacts. Move someone into the pipeline only when they show engagement. 'I want your pipeline to be very much people that you are actively engaging with' (S1 26:17-27:25).

blocks.title: Two warnings
blocks.body:
Closed won means signed. 'You will get salespeople that will mark things as closed won without a contract signed. It does not count.' Decide what closed won means for you: money received, contract signed, or signed plus an onboarding call booked (S1 28:15-28:44).
Write down every concession. A rep promises '10% off if you pay six months up front', writes it nowhere, and at renewal nobody in finance or success knows (S1 29:42-30:00).

rows: Discovery; Demo; Proposal; Negotiation; Closed won / Closed lost
Active; Stalled (no activity in 14+ days); On hold (buyer asked to pause); At risk; or your own, such as 'waiting for the signer'

blocks.title: Why a 'stalled' stage breaks your data
blocks.body: If 'stalled' is a stage, you lose where the deal stopped: was it in demo, proposal or discovery? Keep the stage and set a status, then run a report on all stalled deals by stage (S1 30:25-31:41).

blocks.title: Keep it to 4 to 7 stages
blocks.body: 'If you can't read your stage names on the pipeline board, you have too many stages.' At this stage you do not need more than four to seven (S1 31:45-32:06; slide 17).

rows: MQL = marketing-qualified lead: did something that shows interest (webinar, contact form)
SQL: you decided they fit, e.g. BANT
They want to move forward: a pilot, a contract
Across B2B tech and many markets. Companies define 'opportunity' differently, so compare with care.

blocks.title: Back into your numbers (slides 20-21)
blocks.body: Work backwards from the revenue you want. At $10K a year, $1M of revenue needs 100 deals. With 10 leads to 5 demos to 3 deals, that is about 333 leads and 167 demos. With the benchmarks above, 2 closed deals need about 87 leads, 34 MQLs, 13 SQLs and 5 opportunities. 'Usually people end up being surprised how many leads they actually need' (S1 36:06-37:10). Then find your weakest conversion: wrong traffic at the top, stuck at demo, or too many unqualified people? Those answers become your top-of-funnel goals (S1 37:10-37:46).

blocks.title: Use your own rates
blocks.body: The benchmarks are a starting point. 'Your numbers are definitely going to be different, especially this early. Put your numbers in' (S1 36:51-36:59). The figures are the lecturer's; their source was not given.

blocks.title: Nikos's question: how do MQL and SQL fit our stages? (S1 33:38-36:03)
blocks.body: MQL and SQL mark points inside your stages. Decide where each falls for you: MQL when someone shows interest, SQL when they fit, opportunity when they want to move forward, then closed. Align these with stages named after buyer actions. Too many stages make the tracking meaningless. Brianna offered office hours to map it for each company.

blocks.title: The idea
blocks.body: Weighted value = deal value x stage probability. A $40K deal in Proposal at 50% is worth $20K. 'I have two million dollars in my pipeline' tells an investor nothing; the weighted figure shows how far deals have really moved (S1 39:40-40:44). Márk Máté gave the definition in class: a big amount in prospecting counts for little because only about 5% closes from there (S1 39:12).

blocks.title: Probabilities must come from your own closed deals
blocks.body: Slide 25: 54 closed-won out of 200 that reached Qualification = 27%. Set a probability on each stage in the CRM and recalibrate every quarter against what actually closed. 'If you say we think about 50% close from demo and you don't have any data to show it, then it doesn't matter what you think' (S1 41:45-42:10).

blocks.title: If you are too early
blocks.body: Say so: 'We don't have enough conversion data to assign probabilities yet, but here is what we track instead': how many deals are in proposal, the value of the qualified pipeline, deal sizes and stages. That sounds informed, not like 'throwing numbers out there to look good', which makes investors dig in and stop trusting you (S1 38:16-38:42, 42:13-42:55). A weighted pipeline also tests a goal: can you reach $2M ARR by year end from what is in it? (S1 43:16-43:33)

blocks.title: Expect an ugly first report
blocks.body: Her time-in-stage example showed a contact sitting as a subscriber for 816 days. That is what a first report looks like before cleanup; it tells you where deals sit too long (S1 48:13-48:42; slide 33). ACV = annual contract value; CAC = customer acquisition cost.

blocks.title: CAC in B2B (Márk Máté, S1 55:33-57:04)
blocks.body: People calculate CAC 'based on what makes them look the best'. A true CAC includes sales activity: the sales team's salaries and their tools, not just ad spend moved into overhead. Always say what your CAC includes.

blocks.title: My CRM is in my head: tool first or design first? (Irakli, S1 57:13-58:02)
blocks.body: 'I would put them all in a spreadsheet first, then think about where they're at, and then start designing it.' She offered office hours: 'I know you have 24 hospitals and you have people kind of in different stages with those, with one customer. I'm happy to map out what that looks like.' 'Getting out of your head as soon as possible is probably the most important thing.'

blocks.title: Inbound and outbound acquisition cost (Nikos, S1 58:10-1:00:24)
blocks.body: Tag every deal inbound or outbound. Inbound carries marketing costs; outbound only sales costs. Attribution is fuzzy. Keep one pipeline with the same stages, but report the two separately, because rates differ. Outbound often brings fewer, bigger deals, for example $2,000 a month inbound vs $5,000 a month outbound in her illustration.

pages.title: MediMind: from our 9-step funnel to 6 stages
pages.subtitle: Working hypothesis, not a decision | Based on B3 (2 October) and slides 10, 14, 17

blocks.title: What we have, and the gap
blocks.body: B3 proposed nine steps: target and route in, MQL, SQL, evaluation-ready, parallel delivered, first hands-on test, results reviewed, purchase agreed, approved rollout. Its 'what must be true' rules are already exit criteria, which the lecture wants. Three things do not fit the lecture: nine is above 4-7; 'target' is a contact list, not pipeline (S1 26:17); and 'parallel delivered' is our action, not the buyer's (S1 21:41). Rollout belongs to onboarding, after closed won.

Pain in their words, approval path, next date

Hospital staff completed the agreed workflow hands-on; feedback recorded
Reviewed results against baseline and named who signs, when

blocks.title: Where our own work goes
blocks.body: Our build is a status inside stage 4, not a stage: 'Waiting on us: building', 'Waiting on hospital IT: data access', 'Stalled', 'On hold'. B3's timing targets (14 days from readiness to delivery, 7 days to the first hospital test) then become a time-in-stage report, not extra stages.

pages.title: MediMind: status, numbers and honest investor answers
pages.subtitle: Working hypotheses | slides 16, 25, 38-40 | Nothing has been changed, sent or published

blocks.title: Brianna's '24 hospitals, one customer'
blocks.body: Our notes count GeoHospitals as one buying organization with many sites, not 25 customers (W5D1). So keep two views. The pipeline is one row per new buying organization outside the anchor partner. A separate rollout tracker covers the anchor network's sites: onboarding, not new deals. Mixing them would inflate the pipeline, the first thing investors check: 'Does one customer make up a big share?' (S1 52:31). Check the site count with the founder; she may have meant something else.

rows: Our parallel evaluation is free. Count it as stage 4, never as revenue. Only a signed purchase agreement is closed won.
We have one closed customer. Do not set percentages yet. Say: 'too early to weight; here is the count and value by stage.'
Amount and close date before Proposal (slide 27)
Our price is matched to the hospital's current software spend, so the amount is unknown until we learn it. Make that spend a field captured at Qualified.
Hospitals that said no or went quiet get closed lost with a reason, not left open.
Tag the source: warm introduction, direct outreach or inbound (B2's channels).

blocks.title: Draft answers for an investor today
blocks.body:
Total and weighted pipeline? 'We are too early to weight. We have [n] hospital groups past discovery, [n] qualified and [n] in evaluation.' Fill in from the tracker, never from memory.
Concentration? 'One signed customer, a network of many sites. Our main metric is new hospital groups completing a first hands-on evaluation in the last 30 days' (B3).
Founder-sourced? 'Today mostly founder and warm introductions. We track source so we can show when it becomes repeatable.'

blocks.title: Keep the tracker clean
blocks.body: No patient data, credentials or hospital-confidential documents in the sheet; store approval references and links only (B3). The first-contract value is still unconfirmed (W5D1); check the signed contract before entering any amount.

blocks.title: The sheet (from B3, trimmed)
blocks.body: One row per buying organization: ID; hospital or group; source (warm introduction, direct outreach, inbound) and date; connector, champion, buyer; stage; status; pain (hypothesis or confirmed); current software spend; next step and date; owner; stage-entry dates; lost or stall reason; evidence link. B3's counting rules still apply: distinct buying organizations, first milestones counted once, unknown is not zero.

blocks.title: Why not a CRM tool yet
blocks.body: Brianna's answer to Irakli was a spreadsheet first, and B3 already said one shared tracker is enough to start. With about 15 target accounts (B2), a tool can wait until the stages have survived a month of real use; then the clean data moves over (S1 16:13-16:57).

blocks.title: Questions to take to office hours
blocks.body:
1. Our sale includes a free parallel evaluation of several weeks. Is that one stage (Evaluating) or two, and where does the 'opportunity' start?
2. Our price matches the hospital's current software spend, so the deal amount is unknown early. What should we enter before Proposal?
3. One signed customer with many sites: how should we show expansion at the anchor next to new hospital groups without inflating the pipeline?
4. With only a handful of hospital deals a year, when do stage probabilities become meaningful?
